title: Cognitive overload, an English radio panel game and brain frying.
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Prompted by a newspaper report on a paper about the radio panel game Just A Minute, Skelton uses the show as a vivid picture of cognitive overload: more demands on the brain than the energy available to meet them. He argues that overload is the opposite of the good repeated experiences that make learning sticky, because it cuts off the brain's ability to learn and, repeated, erodes confidence. He illustrates the antidote with the best teacher he ever saw, whose crisp routines, clear instructions and relevant feedback kept overload low and learning high. He extends the point to teachers burdened by badly designed school systems, leaders harmed by inspection, and children arriving already overloaded from home. A clear Hedgehog Concept is presented as a practical way to reduce overload because everyone shares the same focus. The post ends with reflective prompts for ministers, leaders, teachers and parents.
points: Cognitive overload happens when the energy demanded of the brain exceeds what is available, and it directly shuts down the possibility of learning.
The best teacher Skelton observed stood out chiefly for reducing overload through clear routines, a task on the board at entry, crisp instructions and focused feedback.
Overload is not only a student problem; poorly considered school systems and inspection can impose it on teachers and leaders too.
A shared Hedgehog Concept reduces overload because everyone knows what matters and most decisions are filtered through it.
Each group in the system, from ministers to parents, is asked to look for what adds overload and remove it.
quotes: Cognitive Overload happens when the energy we ask the brain to use up is greater than the energy available to it. We all experience cognitive overload at different times.

If good repeated experiences enable the brain to get better by making sticky that which we end up learning, then cognitive overload does the opposite. To quote from the paper, cognitive overload ‘creates a high risk of brain fry’.

In my early days as a teacher, I suspect I may have been very good at creating cognitive overload without realising what I was doing. Since then, I have seen cognitive overload happen hundreds of times in classrooms and organisations.

Her lesson routines were crisp and clear. There was always something on the whiteboard for each of her students to get on with as soon as they came into the classroom, mostly consolidating or developing learning which, in itself, meant that her class was already somewhat familiar with the learning they had been set.

What made her so great - and what her students learned more than any other class in the school - was her ability to get cognitive overload down to the lowest levels. In doing so, she gave her students’ brains maximum energy to learn.

One of the big advantages of a Hedgehog Concept used well is that it helps to diminish cognitive overload by ensuring that everyone - children, parents, colleagues, organisational leaders and others - has the same focus, that everyone knows what really matters and that everyone appreciates that the majority of discussions and decision making will be focused on the Hedgehog Concept. There are reasons why organisations with their own deeply embedded Hedgehog Concept do better than others.
